claim: The Tritonia diomedea swim central pattern generator (CPG) consists of three neuronal types: DSI, C2, and VSI.
source: The Tritonia swim central pattern generator (CPG) consists of three neuronal types: DSI, C2, and VSI (Figure 1A), which form a network oscillator circuit that produces the rhythmic bursting activity (Figure 1B) underlying production of the rhythmic movements (Getting, 1981, 1989b; Katz, 2007a, 2007b, 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work (Getting, 1981, 1989b; Katz, 2007a, 2007b, 2009).

claim: C2 and VSI both send axons through Pedal Nerve 6 (PdN6), which connects the two pedal ganglia.
source: C2 and VSI both send axons through one of the pedal commissures, Pedal Nerve 6 (PdN6), which connects the two pedal ganglia (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C showing the anatomical projection.

claim: Disconnecting PdN6 blocks or seriously impairs the swimming behavior and the motor pattern underlying it.
source: Previously, we reported that disconnecting this commissure blocks or seriously impairs the swimming behavior and the motor pattern underlying it (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).

claim: Cutting PdN6 caused a significant decrease in the number of body flexions 2 hours after surgery compared to sham-operated controls.
source: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA with post-hoc pairwise comparison revealed a significant difference in the number of flexions between cut and sham animals 2 hr after the surgery (p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Prior to cutting PdN6, there was no significant difference between test and sham-operated animals in the number of body flexions.
source: Prior to the cut, there was no significant difference between the test and sham-operated animals in the number of flexions (16 hr, p = 0.57; −12 hr, p = 0.52; −2hr, p = 0.89).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant differences at multiple time points before the lesion.

claim: The coefficient of variance (CoV) of the number of body flexions for transected animals showed a threefold increase after the cut.
source: The coefficient of variance (CoV) of the number of body flexions for the transected animals (gray squares) showed a threefold increase after the cut, but only a slight increase in sham-operated animals (white circles).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2C showing the CoV increase from 0.21 to 0.64.

claim: There is a significant difference in variance between the cut group and the sham group after the surgery.
source: There is a significant difference in variance between the cut group and the sham group after the surgery (by Levene median test, N = 19).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Levene median test) of the experimental data.

claim: Cutting PdN6 revealed greater variability in the population than could be observed under normal conditions.
source: Thus, cutting the commissure revealed a greater variability in the population than could be observed under normal conditions, meaning that some animals were more susceptible to the lesion than others.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed increase in coefficient of variance after the lesion.

claim: Disconnection of PdN6 significantly decreased the number of VSI bursts per swim motor pattern episode.
source: On average, disconnection of PdN6 significantly decreased the number of VSI bursts per swim motor pattern episode (Figure 4B), as shown previously (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and cited previous work (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).

claim: The decrease in VSI bursts after PdN6 disconnection was accompanied by an increased coefficient of variance from 0.16 to 0.47.
source: This decrease was accompanied by an increased CoV from 0.16 to 0.47 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: C2-evoked excitation of VSI is essential for the production of the swim motor pattern.
source: C2-evoked excitation of VSI is essential for the production of the swim motor pattern (Getting, 1983b; Calin-Jageman et al., 2007; Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Getting, 1983b; Calin-Jageman et al., 2007; Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).

claim: Stimulating C2 to fire a train of action potentials induced a burst of action potentials in VSI in 47 out of 53 preparations with PdN6 intact.
source: Stimulating C2 to fire a train of actions potentials (10 Hz for 2 s) induced a burst of action potentials in VSI in 47 out of 53 preparations with PdN6 intact (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 53 preparations.

claim: The C2-evoked VSI spikes were mostly antidromic in 39 out of 47 preparations.
source: The C2-evoked VSI spikes were mostly antidromic, traveling from the pedal ganglion distal to the VSI soma through PdN6 (Figure 5A, N = 39 of 47; cf., Sakurai and Katz, 2009b)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 47 preparations and cited previous work (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).

claim: The number of bursts in the swim motor pattern, under normal conditions, was not correlated with the number of action potentials evoked by C2 when PdN6 was intact.
source: The number of bursts in the swim motor pattern, under normal conditions, was not correlated with the number of action potentials evoked by C2 when PdN6 was intact (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (R2 = 0.05, p = 0.10 by linear regression, N = 52) shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After PdN6 disconnection, there was a significant correlation between the number of VSI bursts per swim episode and the amplitude of the C2-evoked VSI depolarization.
source: After PdN6 disconnection, there was a significant correlation between the number of VSI bursts per swim episode and the amplitude of the C2-evoked VSI depolarization (R2 = 0.53, p< 0.001 by linear regression, N = 50).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The percent change in the number of VSI bursts caused by PdN6 disconnection showed a significant correlation with the amplitude of the C2-evoked depolarization in VSI.
source: The percent change in the number of VSI bursts caused by PdN6 disconnection showed a significant correlation with the amplitude of the C2-evoked depolarization in VSI (p<0.001 by linear regression, R2 = 0.47, p<0.001, N = 50).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The larger the VSI depolarization caused by C2 after PdN6 disconnection, the less impairment there was in the swim motor pattern.
source: Thus, the larger the VSI depolarization caused by C2 after PdN6 disconnection, the less impairment there was in the swim motor pattern.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation data showing that larger depolarizations are associated with less impairment.

claim: C2 stimulation caused a bombardment of small EPSPs in VSI that lasted longer than the duration of stimulation.
source: C2 stimulation caused a bombardment of small EPSPs that lasted longer than the duration of stimulation (black trace).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Recruitment of polysynaptic EPSPs was minimized by superfusion of high-divalent cation (Hi-Di) saline.
source: Recruitment of these polysynaptic EPSPs was minimized by superfusion of high-divalent cation (Hi-Di) saline (gray trace).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In Hi-Di saline, C2 stimulation evoked a smooth biphasic synaptic potential in VSI, with an initial depolarization and a delayed hyperpolarization phase.
source: In Hi-Di saline, C2 stimulation evoked a smooth biphasic synaptic potential in VSI, with an initial depolarization and a delayed hyperpolarization phase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: The hyperpolarizations tended to be larger in amplitude and were more variable than the depolarizations.
source: The hyperpolarizations tended to be larger in amplitude and were more variable (2.9 ± 1.3 mV, N = 32, CoV = 0.66) than the depolarizations (0.8 ± 0.36 mV, N = 32, CoV = 0.42); there was a significant difference in variance between the amplitudes of hyperpolarizations and depolarizations (p< 0.05 by Levene median test, N = 32).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from 32 preparations.

claim: The percent decrease in the number of VSI bursts per swim episode showed a significant inverse correlation with the amplitude of the C2-evoked delayed hyperpolarization in VSI in Hi-Di saline.
source: The percent decrease in the number of VSI bursts per swim episode showed a significant inverse correlation with the amplitude of the C2-evoked delayed hyperpolarization in VSI in Hi-Di saline (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (R2 = 0.44, p<0.001 by linear regression, N = 26) shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Animals in which C2 evoked larger hyperpolarizations in VSI were more vulnerable to having their motor pattern disrupted.
source: These results indicate that the variability in the susceptibility of the motor pattern to PdN6 disconnection originates at least in part from the difference in the extent to which C2 inhibits VSI; animals in which C2 evoked larger hyperpolarizations in VSI were more vulnerable to having their motor pattern disrupted.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation data showing that larger hyperpolarizations are associated with greater impairment.

claim: Out of 69 animals, 17 (24.6%) exhibited only antidromic spike propagation during the swim motor program.
source: Out of 69 animals, 17 (24.6%) exhibited only antidromic spike propagation during the swim motor program in which axonal impulses appeared earlier in PdN6 than in the cell body (Figure 8Ci).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 69 animals.

claim: Five animals (7.2%) showed only orthodromic spikes in which action potentials were generated in or near the pedal ganglion proximal to the VSI soma.
source: In contrast, five animals (7.2%) showed only orthodromic spikes in which action potentials were generated in or near the pedal ganglion proximal to the VSI soma (Figure 8Ciii).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 69 animals.

claim: In 47 animals (68.1%), the direction of VSI spike propagation switched from orthodromic to antidromic, or vice versa, during the swim motor pattern.
source: In 47 animals (68.1%), the direction switched from orthodromic to antidromic, or vice versa, during the swim motor pattern (Figure 8Cii).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 69 animals.

claim: Animals with only orthodromic VSI spikes were significantly less impaired than those with only antidromic VSI spikes.
source: One-way ANOVA with a post-hoc pairwise comparison (Holm-Sidak method) revealed that individuals exhibiting only orthodromic VSI bursts were significantly less impaired than those with only antidromic VSI bursts as indicated by an asterisk (F(2,66) = 4.64, p = 0.015, N = 5 and 16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: VSI tended to show more antidromic spiking later in the swim motor pattern in the majority of animals.
source: VSI tended to show more antidromic spiking later in the swim motor pattern in the majority of animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon blocking PdN6, the motor pattern tended to lose the terminal bursts that contained only antidromic spikes.
source: Upon blocking PdN6, the motor pattern tended to lose the terminal bursts that contained only antidromic spikes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Introducing an artificial inhibitory synaptic conductance in VSI corresponding to the times of C2 spikes caused no change in the number of bursts when PdN6 was intact.
source: Introducing an artificial inhibitory synaptic conductance in VSI corresponding to the times of C2 spikes caused no change in the number of bursts when PdN6 was intact (Figure 9Aii,Bi).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using dynamic clamp shown in Figure 9.

claim: When the artificial inhibitory synaptic conductance was added to the soma by dynamic clamping, all VSI action potentials became antidromic during the swim motor pattern in each of the 16 preparations.
source: When the artificial inhibitory synaptic conductance was added to the soma by dynamic clamping, all VSI action potentials became antidromic during the swim motor pattern in each of the 16 preparations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 16 preparations using dynamic clamp.

claim: Subtraction of the C2-evoked inhibition of VSI significantly increased the number of VSI bursts per swim episode in 6 out of 9 preparations.
source: Subtraction of the C2-evoked inhibition of VSI significantly increased the number of VSI bursts per swim episode in 6 out of 9 preparations (Figure 9Aiii,Ci).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 9 preparations using dynamic clamp shown in Figure 9.

claim: When PdN6 was blocked, addition of the artificial C2 to VSI synaptic inhibition further decreased the number of VSI bursts per swim episode.
source: When PdN6 was blocked, addition of the artificial C2 to VSI synaptic inhibition further decreased the number of VSI bursts per swim episode, making the preparation more susceptible to disconnection of PdN6.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using dynamic clamp shown in Figure 10.

claim: Without dynamic clamp, blocking PdN6 caused a 25% decrease in the number of VSI bursts.
source: On average, without dynamic clamp, blocking PdN6 caused a 25% decrease in the number of VSI bursts (Figure 10Bi, PdN6 blocked).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10Bi.

claim: When the dynamic clamp was turned on after PdN6 blockade, the decrease in VSI bursts became approximately 60% compared to control.
source: When the dynamic clamp was turned on, this became an approximate 60% decrease compared to control (Figure 10Bi, D.C.).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10Bi.

claim: Subtracting the inhibition from C2 to VSI mitigated the effect of disconnecting PdN6.
source: Indeed, subtracting the inhibition from C2 to VSI mitigated the effect of disconnecting PdN6.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using dynamic clamp shown in Figure 10.

claim: When the dynamic clamp was turned on to subtract inhibition, the decreased number of VSI bursts was restored from 27.7% below the control swim motor pattern to 3.3% above the control.
source: When the dynamic clamp was turned on, the decreased number of VSI bursts was restored from 27.7% below the control swim motor pattern to 3.3% above the control, a significant shift (Figure 10Ci).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10Ci with statistical significance (p = 0.003 by paired t-test, N = 19).

claim: Individual animals can exhibit similar behaviors while differing substantially in the properties of the neurons and synapses underlying those behaviors.
source: Experimental and theoretical studies have shown that individual animals can exhibit similar behaviors while differing substantially in the properties of the neurons and synapses underlying those behaviors (Prinz et al., 2004; Goaillard et al., 2009; Calabrese et al., 2011; Norris et al., 2011; Roffman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Prinz et al., 2004; Goaillard et al., 2009; Calabrese et al., 2011; Norris et al., 2011; Roffman et al., 2012).

claim: Individual people differ from one another to such an extent that it can impair the ability to predict outcomes in cases of traumatic brain injury.
source: It has been noted that individual people differ from one another to such an extent that it can impair the ability to predict outcomes in cases of traumatic brain injury (Hukkelhoven et al., 2005; Lingsma et al., 2010; Forsyth and Kirkham, 2012) or stroke (Cramer, 2008a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Hukkelhoven et al., 2005; Lingsma et al., 2010; Forsyth and Kirkham, 2012).

claim: Axonal injury in the white matter plays a complex role in disruption of neural networks underlying higher brain functions.
source: With recent advances in detection techniques, there has been a growing awareness that axonal injury in the white matter plays a complex role in disruption of neural networks underlying higher brain functions (Adams et al., 2000; Schiff et al., 2007; Kinnunen et al., 2011; Squarcina et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Adams et al., 2000; Schiff et al., 2007; Kinnunen et al., 2011; Squarcina et al., 2012).

claim: The escape swim behavior of Tritonia consists of a series of whole body flexions in response to a noxious stimulus.
source: The escape swim behavior of Tritonia consists of a series of whole body flexions in response to a noxious stimulus (Getting, 1989b; Katz, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Getting, 1989b; Katz, 2009).

claim: Differences in synaptic properties, which were of no consequence under ordinary conditions, caused different outcomes when the circuit was challenged with an injury.
source: In this study, we report that differences in synaptic properties, which were of no consequence under ordinary conditions, caused different outcomes when the circuit was challenged with an injury.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript showing that synaptic variability affects lesion susceptibility.

claim: Subtle differences between animals within the neural circuit underlying swimming behavior had no behavioral relevance under normal conditions but caused differential vulnerability of the behavior to a particular brain lesion.
source: We found that in the mollusc, Tritonia diomedea, subtle differences between animals within the neural circuit underlying swimming behavior had no behavioral relevance under normal conditions but caused differential vulnerability of the behavior to a particular brain lesion.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The extent of motor impairment correlated with the site of spike initiation in VSI, which was determined by the strength of an inhibitory synapse onto this neuron.
source: The extent of motor impairment correlated with the site of spike initiation in a specific neuron in the neural circuit, which was determined by the strength of an inhibitory synapse onto this neuron.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding of the study based on experimental data showing correlations between inhibitory synapse strength, spike initiation site, and motor impairment.

claim: Artificially increasing or decreasing the inhibitory synaptic conductance with dynamic clamp correspondingly altered the extent of motor impairment by the lesion without affecting normal operation.
source: Artificially increasing or decreasing this inhibitory synaptic conductance with dynamic clamp correspondingly altered the extent of motor impairment by the lesion without affecting normal operation.
evidence: The claim summarizes the dynamic clamp experiments showing that manipulating the inhibitory synapse affects lesion susceptibility but not normal function.

claim: Neural circuit differences could serve as hidden phenotypes for predicting the behavioral outcome of neural damage.
source: The results suggest that neural circuit differences could serve as hidden phenotypes for predicting the behavioral outcome of neural damage.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C2-evoked synaptic response of VSI contained both monosynaptic and polysynaptic components.
source: The C2-evoked synaptic response of VSI contained both monosynaptic and polysynaptic components (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In 47 out of 56 preparations, the C2 to VSI synaptic response was a mix of both depolarization and hyperpolarization.
source: In 47 out of 56 preparations, it was a mix of both depolarization and hyperpolarization (cf., Figure 6Biii, Animal 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 56 preparations.

claim: In four preparations, C2 stimulation caused only depolarization with multiple components.
source: In the remaining four preparations, C2 stimulation caused only depolarization with multiple components (cf., Figure 6Biv, Animal 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 56 preparations.

claim: The excitation of the proximal VSI process was mainly caused by a bombardment of recruited EPSPs that overrode the direct synaptic action of C2 onto VSI.
source: Getting (1989a) suggested that C2 excites VSI via direct synaptic action, but we found that the excitation of the proximal VSI process was mainly caused by a bombardment of recruited EPSPs that overrode the direct synaptic action of C2 onto VSI (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and contrasts with previous suggestions (Getting, 1989a).

claim: The polysynaptic recruitment did not appear to play a major role in causing the individual differences in the extent of motor impairment after PdN6 disconnection.
source: However, the polysynaptic recruitment did not appear to play a major role in causing the individual differences in the extent of motor impairment after PdN6 disconnection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the inhibitory component, not the polysynaptic excitation, was predictive of impairment.

claim: The inhibitory component of the direct synaptic action by C2 onto VSI was more significant in predicting the susceptibility to the lesion.
source: Rather, it was the inhibitory component of the direct synaptic action by C2 onto VSI that was more significant in predicting the susceptibility to the lesion (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7 demonstrating correlation between inhibitory component and lesion susceptibility.

claim: Stronger inhibition would counteract the depolarizing effect of recruited polysynaptic EPSPs in VSI and hence make the system more susceptible to loss of the distal spike initiation zone.
source: Stronger inhibition would counteract the depolarizing effect of recruited polysynaptic EPSPs in VSI and hence make the system more susceptible to loss of the distal spike initiation zone.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic inference based on the experimental findings about the role of inhibition.

claim: Adding artificial inhibition did not affect the production of the motor pattern with PdN6 intact.
source: Importantly, it did not affect the production of the motor pattern with PdN6 intact.
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamic clamp experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: This synaptic difference serves as a hidden phenotype that predicts the susceptibility of the neural circuit to disruption.
source: Thus, this synaptic difference serves as a hidden phenotype that predicts the susceptibility of the neural circuit to disruption.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing that the synapse affects lesion susceptibility but not normal function.

claim: Subtraction of the C2 to VSI inhibition using dynamic clamp partly rescued vulnerable preparations from the effects of the lesion.
source: Subtracting the C2 to VSI inhibition using dynamic clamp partly rescued vulnerable preparations from the effects of the lesion.
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamic clamp experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Artificial reduction of the inhibitory synaptic conductance would enhance C2-evoked depolarization through bombardment of recruited EPSPs, which would make the proximal spike initiation zone of VSI more excitable.
source: This is likely because artificial reduction of the inhibitory synaptic conductance would enhance C2-evoked depolarization through bombardment of recruited EPSPs, which would make the proximal spike initiation zone of VSI more excitable.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic inference explaining the observed effects of subtracting inhibition.

claim: VSI has two spike initiation zones, one in each pedal ganglion, where C2 synaptic actions take place.
source: VSI has two spike initiation zones, one in each pedal ganglion, where C2 synaptic actions take place (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).

claim: The proximal and distal spike-initiation zones each are capable of initiating spikes; however, firing of either zone produces spikes in the same axon but with different directions of propagation.
source: The proximal and distal spike-initiation zones each are capable of initiating spikes; however, firing of either zone produces spikes in the same axon but with different directions of propagation (Figure 8; Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and cited previous work (Sakurai and Katz, 2009b).

claim: The presence of multiple spike-initiation zones made the circuit more resilient to a lesion by providing a backup spike-initiation zone after loss of the primary spike-initiation zone when the commissure was disconnected.
source: In this study, we directly showed that the presence of multiple spike-initiation zones made the circuit more resilient to a lesion by providing a backup spike-initiation zone after loss of the primary spike-initiation zone when the commissure was disconnected.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about spike initiation zones and lesion susceptibility.

claim: The susceptibility of the motor pattern to lesion was apparently dependent on the location of the primary spike initiation zone in VSI.
source: Thus, the susceptibility of the motor pattern to lesion was apparently dependent on the location of the primary spike initiation zone in VSI.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between spike initiation direction and lesion susceptibility.

claim: If spikes originated in the proximal region of VSI, PdN6 disconnection would have less effect on the swim performance.
source: If spikes originated in the proximal region of VSI, PdN6 disconnection would have less effect on the swim performance.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic inference based on the experimental findings about spike initiation zones.

claim: The strength of the inhibitory component of the C2-to-VSI synapse does not affect the function of the intact swim circuit under normal conditions, but may determine its susceptibility to the lesion.
source: The results above suggest that the strength of the inhibitory component of the C2-to-VSI synapse does not affect the function of the intact swim circuit under normal conditions, but may determine its susceptibility to the lesion.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, particularly the dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: Severe loss of brain function is often caused by a complex pattern of diffuse axonal injury in the white matter that are critical nodes for distributed network functions.
source: Severe loss of brain function is often caused by a complex pattern of diffuse axonal injury in the white matter that are critical nodes for distributed network functions (Adams et al., 2000; Schiff et al., 2007; Kinnunen et al., 2011; Squarcina et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Adams et al., 2000; Schiff et al., 2007; Kinnunen et al., 2011; Squarcina et al., 2012).

claim: Stroke can cause axonal lesions in subcortical white matter.
source: Stroke can also cause axonal lesions in subcortical white matter (Bamford et al., 1991; Sozmen et al., 2009; Blasi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work (Bamford et al., 1991; Sozmen et al., 2009; Blasi et al., 2014).

claim: Disruption of axonal pathways that link nodes in the distributed brain networks would cause motor deficits and cognitive/learning disabilities, which are commonly seen in children with cerebral palsy.
source: Disruption of axonal pathways that link nodes in the distributed brain networks would cause motor deficits and cognitive/learning disabilities, which are commonly seen in children with cerebral palsy (Riddle et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Riddle et al., 2012).

claim: This is the first direct analysis of synaptic variation affecting vulnerability of a neuronal circuit to a particular lesion.
source: To our knowledge this is the first direct analysis of synaptic variation affecting vulnerability of a neuronal circuit to a particular lesion.
evidence: The claim is a statement by the authors about the novelty of their work based on their knowledge of the literature.

claim: The magnitude of C2-evoked polysynaptic excitation of VSI is more likely determined by the amplitude of C2-evoked hyperpolarization phase, which limits the depolarizing effect of the recruited polysynaptic EPSPs in VSI in normal saline.
source: Thus, the magnitude of C2-evoked polysynaptic excitation of VSI is more likely determined by the amplitude of C2-evoked hyperpolarization phase, which limits the depolarizing effect of the recruited polysynaptic EPSPs in VSI in normal saline.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amplitude of C2-evoked depolarization in normal saline showed no correlation with the amplitude of the depolarizing phase recorded in Hi-Di saline.
source: Indeed, the amplitude of C2-evoked depolarization in normal saline (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, inset next to y axis) showed no correlation with the amplitude of the depolarizing phase recorded in Hi-Di saline (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (R2 = 0.04, p=0.37 by linear regression, N = 24) shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The amplitude of C2-evoked depolarization in normal saline showed a significant inverse correlation with the amplitude of the hyperpolarization phase.
source: whereas it showed a significant inverse correlation with the amplitude of the hyperpolarization phase (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (R2 = 0.43, p<0.001 by linear regression, N = 24) shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Before dynamic clamping, orthodromic VSI action potentials were detected in 50% of the preparations during the swim motor pattern.
source: Before dynamic clamping, orthodromic VSI action potentials were detected in 50% of the preparations during the swim motor pattern (N = 8 of 16).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 16 preparations.

claim: Enhanced hyperpolarization in the soma suppresses orthodromic spiking in VSI, but the distal VSI terminal is still able to generate antidromic bursts.
source: This indicates that enhanced hyperpolarization in the soma suppresses orthodromic spiking in VSI, but the distal VSI terminal is still able to generate antidromic bursts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dynamic clamp experiments showing that adding inhibition converts all spikes to antidromic.

claim: Under conditions where inhibition was subtracted, all VSI bursts contained orthodromic action potentials in all 16 preparations.
source: Under such conditions, all VSI bursts contained orthodromic action potentials in all 16 preparations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 16 preparations using dynamic clamp.

claim: With PdN6 intact, additional synaptic inhibition from C2 to VSI did not affect the number of bursts in the motor pattern; it acted like a hidden change in the circuit.
source: Thus, with PdN6 intact, additional synaptic inhibition from C2 to VSI did not affect the number of bursts in the motor pattern; it acted like a hidden change in the circuit.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Subtraction of the inhibitory conductance extended the motor pattern by causing more orthodromic spiking.
source: In contrast, subtraction of the inhibitory conductance extended the motor pattern by causing more orthodromic spiking.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: The number of C2 bursts was largely unaffected by dynamic clamp, probably because the artificial conductance was applied to only one of bilateral VSI pair and C2 is electrically coupled to its contralateral counterpart.
source: The number of C2 bursts was largely unaffected, probably because the artificial conductance was applied to only one of bilateral VSI pair and C2 is electrically coupled to its contralateral counterpart.
evidence: The claim is an inference explaining why C2 bursts were not affected by the manipulation.

claim: After PdN6 disconnection, addition of inhibitory synaptic current significantly decreased the number of bursts.
source: Thus, after PdN6 disconnection, addition of inhibitory synaptic current significantly decreased the number of bursts.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using dynamic clamp shown in Figure 10.

claim: Artificial enhancement of C2-to-VSI inhibition made the swim motor pattern more susceptible to disruption caused by PdN6 disconnection.
source: Thus, artificial enhancement of C2-to-VSI inhibition made the swim motor pattern more susceptible to disruption caused by PdN6 disconnection.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 10.

claim: The effect of subtracting the inhibition tended to be more effective in the more vulnerable preparations, which increased the number of bursts by one.
source: The effect of subtracting the inhibition tended to be more effective in the more vulnerable preparations, which increased the number of bursts by one (Figure 10Cii).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10Cii.

claim: Subtracting the inhibitory component of the C2 to VSI synapse restored the impaired swim motor pattern after PdN6 disconnection.
source: Thus, subtracting the inhibitory component of the C2 to VSI synapse restored the impaired swim motor pattern after PdN6 disconnection.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 10.
